quote.text:
Uncle Bob just put out a pretty cool viewer for proposed changes from agents here.

I broke down what he has built and it's system for improving design and planning with agents.

The first image describes his design and the system he is proposing. It's super cool and should make designing with agents better, especially when evaluating proposed changes.

The one big quibble I have is the current implementation is coupled to Grok. I believe that something like this should be able to layer onto any harness, and should be extensible.

The second image shows my proposal for how it could be made harness agnostic.

I'm building out a similar implementation inspired by his on my harness today, which already has a custom plan card and flow and could really benefit from a dedicated visual flow.

I would love to make an issue and propose a change to Bob's library to drive compatibility like this in the future. Then I could refactor my harness to use it instead of maintaining an inspired copy.

https://agent-harness.jakeselby.com

results.text:
Of course younguns think that UML is ancient and deprecated -- something we've outgrown.  

That's funny.  

What we've actually outgrown is the use of UML as an up-front specification language.  What we have not outgrown, and likely will not outgrow any time soon, is a need to recursively depict the structure of a software system.   

And it turns out that UML class diagrams (e.g. E-R diagrams) are uniquely applicable for such purposes.

results.text:
Given that agents still need high level supervision.  And given that the human review of code is a bottleneck.  And given that the models have gotten good enough that strict deterministic harnesses are suboptimal.  

Then how should we supervise their output.

My current solution is to use an interrogation tool coupled with an agent.  The tool displays the structure of the system in a UML-like diagram, color coded with crap and mutation scores.  The diagram is dynamic, allowing the user to click on element and drill down through the architecture -- all the way to code.  

The user can detect structures that need improvement and tell the associated agent to make the appropriate changes.  These changes can range from high level architectural changes, to the lowest level code refactorings.  The associated agent will make those changes and cause them to be redisplayed.

The tool I'm using is custom made for me, but you can point an agent at it and use it as a template to build your own custom tool.

It's a work in progress, so don't be surprised if it changes a lot over the next few weeks.  But then you probably won't care because by then you'll be deep in customizing it for yourself.  And anyway, you can always point an agent back at mine, or someone else's, and integrate improvements into your own.

http://github.com/unclebob/uml-viewer.
